Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital payment systems.  21 variables in 4 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: Evidence of partial refugee/migrant access: AFI notes Bank of Tanzania worked with government and FIU on National Risk Assessment to identify risks posed by refugees and develop tiered KYC processes within NFIF 2.0, and that BoT empowers banks/MNOs to develop products suitable for forcibly displaced persons, indicating some enabling work but not full nationwide access guarantee. ([Alliance for Financial Inclusion - Forcibly Displaced Persons thematic page](https://www.afi-global.org/old/thematic-areas/forcibly-displaced-persons/));([UNCDF Tanzania refugee financial education toolkit](https://www.uncdf.org/article/5659/tanzania---a-financial-education-toolkit-designed-for-refugees-and-host-communities))
revision_notes: Both cited sources fetched and read. The AFI thematic page is a generic global landing page for the Forcibly Displaced Persons workstream with no Tanzania-specific regulatory content, and the UNCDF toolkit article describes a financial-literacy pilot in refugee camps rather than the legal basis for account access - neither source directly substantiates the Comments text on NFIF 2.0/tiered KYC. A more specific and authoritative source (UNHCR Innovation Service, 'Displaced and Disconnected: East and Horn of Africa and Great Lakes Region', July 2022) was located and confirms the substance of the score: Tanzania's Electronic Money Regulations 2015 set a tiered KYC/CDD framework that grants refugees and asylum-seekers easy, ID-free access to the lowest-tier mobile money account for simple transfers, but cash-in requires an undefined 'acceptable photo ID' and cash-out requires forms of ID (voter's card, employment ID, social security ID, ward/village letter) that refugees are unlikely to hold, effectively blocking full functional use. Tanzania is grouped with Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi and Somalia as lacking the more refugee-friendly tiered KYC seen in Ethiopia, South Sudan and Uganda. This supports Partial (2) rather than No (1) or Yes (3): a legal pathway exists for basic transfers but full account functionality (cash-in/cash-out) is not practically accessible. Score confirmed unchanged; sources replaced with the more directly relevant UNHCR report.
revised_comments: Refugees and asylum-seekers in Tanzania have partial legal access to digital payment accounts. Tanzania's Electronic Money Regulations 2015 establish a tiered KYC/CDD framework under which the lowest-tier mobile money account can be opened for simple transfers without formal identity documentation, giving refugees and asylum-seekers a practical entry point to mobile money. However, conducting cash-in transactions requires an 'acceptable photo ID' and cash-out requires specific documents (voter's registration, employment ID, social security ID, or a letter from a ward/village executive) that most refugees and asylum-seekers are unable to obtain, which restricts full use of the account. The Bank of Tanzania's National Financial Inclusion Framework has also flagged forcibly displaced persons as a group requiring tailored risk-based KYC approaches. Overall, access is enabled at the margins but not comprehensive.
